While reviewing #481112 I noticed many GRUB failures, all of which were just test bugs.

See each commit for an explanation but in short:

  • switch the terminal type to "dumb", so it renders plainly on qemu stdout, rather than outputting GRUB's terminal escape characters

items.title: nixos/gokapi: build more consistent with upstream

items.content_html:
Motivation and summary

Simple mistakes like forgetting a ; when writing nginx configs can take down all your sites.

This is because the nginx -t test command is being executed in the preStart of the systemd service. Moving this check to build time avoids these accidental small down times.

Fixes #35395.

Prior work

This has been attempted previously in #205561, but it caused some issues and was reverted in #209075.
The main issues were nginx -t being impure: it tried to access the internet to resolve hosts, and tried to read SSL certificates on the disk, which are not available in the nix sandbox.

(A gixy check was added in #57979, it makes the config fail to build if it finds security issues, but it doesn't detect syntax errors.)

Implementation

To combat the previous issues, I created an nginx patch that adds a new -S flag, which behaves like -T, but is skips the impure checks.

Testing

Manually tested this with our config which has proxyPass option with a remote domain that requires internet access to resolve, and of course we have SSL certificates. Syntax validation passes with the current config, and fails with eg. removing a ;.

I'd be happy to add automatic tests, but not sure what's the best approach. The problem is NixOS tests are for runtime asserts, some lib tests that I've met are eval time, what about build time assertions? Is a bash script (with eg. expect) next to the nginx NixOS test preferred, or converting the build time failure to eval time with IFD (I know it's disallowed for regular uses, not sure about tests)?

items.content_html:
Description of changes

While profiling NixOS rebuilds, I noticed that build-composefs-dump.py takes a measurable amount of time (around 100ms). If a user has etc as overlayfs enabled, the script is executed every time they modify anything in /etc. I think this makes it significant enough to want to avoid this delay, so I rewrote the script in Rust. The new implementation closely mirrors the previous one and it has exactly the same output. On my machine with 180 entries in /etc, it takes less than 10ms.

I took inspiration from switch-to-configuration-ng and includes the source directly in nixpkgs next to its package.nix. The package includes NixOS tests for etc as overlayfs which the old python script didn't.

Possible disadvantages:

  • The package must be present to rebuild a system (556KB vs. 7KB for the old script assuming python is present)
  • This script may not be appropriate to be included as a package
  • May be harder to read or modify

I've been daily driving this successfully for a few months and got the idea to upstream it. I'd really appreciate feedback.

@nikstur (original author of build-composefs-dump.py)

items.content_html:
Container runtimes like Docker and Podman disable the unshare system call as a security precaution. A hard-coded use of unshare prevents repart-image from working in such sandboxed environments.

This change lets consumers opt out from remapping the root user on the kernel side. It should be safe to disable if the image only uses userspace tools, but may break images using kernel-space filesystem drivers like btrfs.

Note: I'm not quite sure how to test this option without introducing too much duplication. nixos/tests/appliance-repart-image-verity-store.nix builds successfully with useUnshare = false, but we probably want to test building an image with it enabled as well.

items.content_html:
When stub-ld was first merged, there were some significant issues caused by the build closure size, which were ultimately mostly solved by #398449, though this was obviously a sub-optimal solution.

While studying the newly-hooked-up minimal bootstrap chain, I realized the M2 compiler from stage0-posix had everything I actually needed to make the stub-ld executables, including for i686 binaries on x86_64 systems, with zero additional build closure beyond what was already needed for stdenv.

Effectively reverts:

  • #398449
  • #457909

On the systems supported by stage0-posix (which includes everything built by hydra):

  • Makes no use of secondary nixpkgs instantiations, keeping eval costs small.
  • Shares its build closure completely with stdenv (even if it didn't, it could be bootstrapped in a few seconds). This is the case even when building the i686 binary on x86_64 systems.

On other systems:

  • Uses pkgsStatic, as it did before this PR.

Closes #373776

items.content_html:
Summary

Adds services.vanguards, a NixOS module for the Tor Project's vanguards
add-on. It attaches to a running Tor instance's control port and manages the extra guard
layers ("Full Vanguards") that the Tor specification
says SHOULD be available for long-lived onion services:

"Full Vanguards is intended for use by long-lived onion services, which intend to remain
in operation for longer than one month."

The vanguards package has been in nixpkgs since January 2025 (pkgs/by-name/va/vanguards),
but no NixOS module for it exists in nixpkgs - services.tor runs an onion service that stays
up indefinitely with no way to declare this defense.

The bad news first, because a module that doesn't say it isn't honest

  • Upstream (mikeperry-tor/vanguards) has not pushed since July 2024. Its author has not
    responded to #99 or
    #100, both open since November 2023.
  • There is a documented interaction bug, tpo/core/tor#40892,
    "Tor 0.4.8.9 broken in combination with vanguards" - the documented workaround is stopping
    vanguards and restarting Tor (systemctl stop vanguards && systemctl restart tor@default),
    not just restarting vanguards. I checked the Tor ChangeLog from 0.4.8.9 through the
    0.4.9.11 nixpkgs currently ships (searched for "40892", "guard", "consensus" and
    "microdesc" across every 0.4.8.x/0.4.9.x entry) and found no fix that addresses this bug -
    that is not proof it still reproduces, but there is no changelog evidence that it doesn't.
  • Whonix has already declared the add-on unmaintained and closed a mirrored bug
    (QubesOS/qubes-issues#8726) on
    2026-05-21 with "Vanguards abandoned upstream (...) No longer relevant. Closing."
  • Tor's own vanguards-lite, built into Tor since 0.4.7, already covers short-lived
    services and clients.     This module only matters for the case vanguards-lite explicitly
    does not cover: onion services that stay up for more than a month.

None of this makes the module wrong to add - the spec still says SHOULD, and there is no
alternative way to get Full Vanguards on the Tor C implementation - but a PR that omitted it
would be misleading about what a services.vanguards.enable = true; actually buys someone
today.

What the module does

  • services.vanguards.enable, .package, .settings (free-form INI, matching
    vanguards' own SafeConfigParser-based config file - see vanguards-example.conf
    upstream for the ~30 keys across 5 sections; nothing needs to be set to get sane defaults)
  • Runs as User = "tor"; Group = "tor" (not DynamicUser) - see "How this was tested" below
    for why
  • Connects via --control_socket /run/tor/control, the same socket
    services.tor.controlSocket.enable already creates - no new Tor-side wiring needed beyond
    turning CookieAuthentication on (the module does this with mkDefault)
  • bindsTo = [ "tor.service" ]: stops when the Tor instance it is protecting stops, rather
    than idling against a dead control port
  • An assertions entry requiring services.tor.controlSocket.enable, with a message
    explaining why

How this was tested

A NixOS VM test (nixos/tests/vanguards.nix) boots a single machine with services.tor (an
onion service, controlSocket.enable) and services.vanguards.enable, then checks that
vanguards.service becomes active, authenticates against the control port (grepping the
journal for vanguards' own success message, "connected to Tor", and asserting the absence
of "Unable to authenticate"), and reports its systemd-analyze security score.

The first version of the module used DynamicUser = true; SupplementaryGroups = [ "tor" ];.
It passed those checks - and the rest of the journal, read in full rather than just grepped
for the success line, showed Errno 13: Permission denied reading
/var/lib/tor/cached-microdesc-consensus. vanguards reads Tor's cached consensus directly
off disk to compute guard weights, not only through the control port, and Tor's own
StateDirectoryMode is 0700 - group membership authenticates but does not grant that read.
Switching to User = "tor"; Group = "tor" (matching how upstream itself assumes vanguards is
deployed, and how Whonix/Qubes run it) fixed this without adding any new access path into
Tor's state directory.

What the test does not prove: with only one machine and no directory authority, this
network never produces a real consensus, so guard selection itself is unverified here - the
journal still shows Tor retrying to fetch descriptors (Errno 2, not Errno 13 -
file-not-found, not a permission problem, and expected in an isolated test network). This is
noted directly in test.nix. Proving guard selection would need a heavier test with real
directory authorities, the way nixos/tests/tor.nix does - out of scope for this PR.

Why I'm asking for review from @ju1m specifically

You're the listed maintainer for services.tor, and this module is a thin companion to it
rather than something that stands alone. If you'd rather have it as
services.tor.vanguards.* inside tor.nix instead of a sibling module, say so and I'll fold
it in.

Disclosure: this module, its NixOS test, and this PR description were drafted with LLM
assistance (Claude Sonnet 5, via Claude Code), in a session I directed and reviewed. I'm
accountable for what's in this PR; where review raises something I haven't already worked
through, I'll say so and go find the answer rather than guess.

items.content_html:
Description of changes

When the redirect check fails, every remedy the error message offers assumes the
reader is working inside a nixpkgs checkout:

    Added new content?
        $ redirects add-content <identifier> <path>
...
    NOTE: Run the right nix-shell to make this command available.
        Nixpkgs:
        $ nix-shell doc
        NixOS:
        $ nix-shell nixos/doc/manual

NOTE: If your build passes locally and you see this message in CI, you probably
need a rebase.

But the check is also reachable from an ordinary NixOS configuration: any
out-of-tree module setting meta.doc contributes an identifier that
nixos/doc/manual/redirects.json cannot list, so nixos-manual-html fails and
nixos-rebuild stops. This was reported in #412451 and resolved in #412731 by
adding documentation.nixos.checkRedirects.

That option is the right escape hatch, but nothing in the error message points
to it, so a user who hits this has no way to get from the failure to the fix.
This adds one note:

    NOTE: Building a NixOS configuration rather than working on nixpkgs itself?
        An out-of-tree module that sets `meta.doc` contributes identifiers that
        nixos/doc/manual/redirects.json cannot list. Skip this check with the
        NixOS option:

            documentation.nixos.checkRedirects = false;

No behaviour change -- the text of one existing error message only.

Reproducer

mymod.md:

# My Fake Thing {#module-services-myfakething}

mymod.nix:

{ lib, ... }:
{
  options.services.myFakeThing.enable = lib.mkEnableOption "my fake thing";
  meta.doc = ./mymod.md;
}

Adding mymod.nix to a configuration and building
config.system.build.manual.manualHTML fails with
module-services-myfakething. Confirmed on nixos-26.05 (a9e6d84) and
nixos-unstable (2c423e0).

Things done

  • Built on platform(s): x86_64-linux
  • Text-only change to an existing diagnostic; no functional change.
